families.source: UKHSA basic concepts of radiation guidance
families.topic: ionising and non-ionising radiation, exposure pathways and health effects
evidence_points: Radiation is the transfer of energy from one place to another.
Radiation is grouped broadly into ionising and non-ionising forms.
Visible light, radio waves and mobile-phone signals are examples of non-ionising radiation.
X-rays and emissions from uranium ore are examples of ionising radiation.
The page explains how radiation can affect people.
It describes common ways people may be exposed to radiation.

families.source: Defra guidance on using the Daily Air Quality Index
families.topic: daily forecasts, short-term health risk bands and the five pollutants used by the DAQI
families.page_title: Using the Daily Air Quality Index (DAQI)
evidence_points: Defra provides daily forecasts to help people understand and reduce short-term exposure.
The DAQI communicates pollution risk using words, numbers and colours.
Levels 1 to 3 are low, 4 to 6 moderate, 7 to 9 high and 10 very high.
Health advice is provided for the general population and more sensitive groups.
The index covers PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide, ozone and sulphur dioxide.
A location’s score is based on the highest measured or forecast level among the five pollutants.

families.page_title: Health advice for the Daily Air Quality Index (DAQI)
evidence_points: The page provides health advice for low, moderate, high and very high pollution.
It distinguishes advice for the general public from advice for sensitive groups.
Sensitive groups include adults and children with heart or lung conditions and older people.
Short-term exposure over hours or days can cause health effects.
Advice becomes more protective as the DAQI band increases.
People should use symptoms, medical advice and local forecasts when deciding how to modify activity.
